newsitem.title: Zaire: U.S. moves towards backing for Zaire force.
newsitem.headline: U.S. moves towards backing for Zaire force.

text.p: The United States moved closer on Wednesday to approving U.S. military involvement in a relief operation in eastern Zaire, but details of what the force would be empowered to do remained sketchy.
In Kigali, Rwanda's president warned the intervention could go the way of other ill-fated missions to Africa unless Zairean rebels were consulted.

White House spokesman Mike McCurry said President Bill Clinton discussed the refugee crisis with other world leaders, including Canadian Prime Minister Jean Chretien whose government has offered to lead a multinational force to the region.

The mission of the proposed force would be to aid starving refugees in eastern Zaire who have been fleeing fighting between Tutsi rebels and Zaire's army, but it was not clear if the force would be able to disarm well-armed Hutu thugs.
In an ominous development, Uganda reported it had repulsed an attack by Zairean soldiers and Zaire-based Ugandan dissidents on two border posts in the southwest of the country.

In a statement in the name of the Ugandan cabinet, minister of state for international cooperation Martin Aliker said Uganda had repulsed the "enemy" and the Zairean soldiers and Ugandan dissidents retreated into Zaire from where they had shelled Ugandan positions all day.

Uganda has close links with the Tutsi-led government in Kigali which in turn support the Zairean rebels. Regional experts have long feared the crisis in Central Africa could escalate unless it is quickly contained.

McCurry said before committing U.S. troops Clinton wanted to reconcile "different objectives and different ideas presented by different nations" and seek the support of African countries whose interests might be affected.
Rwanda's President Pasteur Bizimungu told Reuters the United Nations had not yet consulted the Banyamulenge rebel force now controlling eastern Zaire and the key airports of Bukavu, Uvira and Goma.
"If they do not negotiate this with the rebels then they will be declaring war and it will be messy," the president, a member of the Hutu majority, added in an interview.

U.S. military intervention in Somalia from December 1992 followed by a full U.N. multinational force turned bloody in 1993 when the U.S. military came into conflict with rag-tag militia forces of late Somali warlord Mohamed Farah Aideed.

In Rome, U.S. Agriculture Secretary Dan Glickman said the United States was ready to provide humanitarian aid and support to refugees in Africa's Great Lakes region as soon as the right mechanisms could be established.

Glickman made the announcement at the World Food Summit without spelling out whether such support would be in the form of participation in a multinational force being organised to confront the crisis in eastern Zaire.

Meanwhile on the ground aid workers resumed distribution on Wednesday of the first outside supplies to reach east Zaire since fighting began, after shelling of the hospital in Goma town had sent them running for cover.

Held up by two days of talks with suspicious local rebels, a group of U.N. and other agencies had finally begun to unload 10 tonnes of food and supplies when shells slammed into and near the hospital compound. No injuries were reported.
"It is a signal of what things could be like if we want to mount a major operation in Goma," said Michelle Quintaglie, a U.N. World Food Programe (WFP) spokeswoman.

But she said sending aid from Rwanda via Goma to 1.2 million stranded refugees was still the only real option. A U.N. plan to send it through remote Kisangani, deep in Zaire on the other side on the frontline, was unfeasible.
"It would be a logistical nightmare," Quintaglie said.
